question_text: Lithium carbonate is less stable to heat than the other alkali metal carbonates. Explain.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The reason
lines: The other alkali metal carbonates are
stable to heat and do not decompose
The Li⁺ ion is the smallest alkali metal
ion, so its polarising power is very high.
It polarises the large CO₃²⁻ ion strongly
and weakens the C–O bonds inside it.
So Li₂CO₃ decomposes at a much lower
steps.why: The thermal stability of a carbonate depends on how strongly the cation pulls at the carbonate ion. A small cation with high polarising power distorts the carbonate ion and weakens its C–O bonds, so less heat is needed to break it into the oxide and carbon dioxide.
common_mistakes: Writing that Li⁺ is large. It is the smallest of the alkali metal ions, and that small size is the reason for the answer.
Stopping at the statement that lithium is different. The answer needs the polarisation of the large carbonate ion by the small Li⁺ ion.
steps.memory_tip: Small ion, strong pull, weak C–O bond, early decomposition.
steps.margin_note: Name the small size of Li⁺ and the polarisation of the carbonate ion.

steps.label: The equation
steps.why: The carbonate ion breaks into an oxide ion and carbon dioxide, so the products are lithium oxide and carbon dioxide gas. The equation is balanced as written: two lithium, one carbon and three oxygen atoms on each side.
common_mistakes: Writing LiOH or Li₂O₂ as the product. Heating the carbonate gives the oxide Li₂O and CO₂.
Writing LiO for lithium oxide. Lithium is +1 and oxygen is −2, so the formula is Li₂O.
steps.memory_tip: Take carbon dioxide away from the carbonate and the oxide is what is left.
steps.margin_note: Write the balanced equation under the reason; the products are the oxide and carbon dioxide.

insider_note: A complete answer has two parts — the small size and high polarising power of Li⁺, and the balanced equation for the decomposition.
